## Owner decision — an ordinary session before the rescue relabel is confirmed, 2026-11-03

Scope: a machine recovered under decision B on this bead, without a recovery sheet, whose relabel to the new id (for example, `b-7`) has not been confirmed by a captured readback. This answers the second open owner question in the common-fact record on this bead titled "Technical common fact — the ordinary session after a partial sheetless recovery": which machine id a bound session sees in that window, and whether an ordinary session may bind before confirmation. Decision B already says "Confirmed label/current-ID status needs the captured installed-system readback following the selected new-key login", and that `b-7` is shown "as the proposed or pending destination after acceptance".

Selected, as an amendment:
- While the bounded recovery flow runs, no ordinary session binds the machine, as in Replace's flow, which runs "in a model-free harness flow — no session is bound and no model sees either key".
- Once that flow has stopped unfinished, for example after the changed-label A stop, the operator may bind an ordinary session through `SEC-1`'s re-entry, which binds "on a maintained machine only".
- The model is shown the pending id, for example `b-7`, marked unconfirmed, with each label the harness has read from the disk beside it as an as-of observation. Decision B already says that once a write has been sent, the earlier observed `a-7` "is only an as-of observation, not an assertion about the disk's current label". No observed label becomes the machine's id: "A disk label is never adopted automatically", and changed-label A still holds: "adopt no `9` and invent no installation boundary".
- In the install brief, on a machine whose relabel is unconfirmed, a root whose label does not equal the shown id is surfaced to the operator. It is never erased as the predecessor, and never resumed or treated as found complete, until a destructive reinstall of this machine is dispatched. This narrows, for this window only, the brief's rule that "An unmarked or foreign-id root is the approved predecessor, not a resume".
- At that dispatch the boundary moves as `STG-20` already says: the separately approved destructive reinstall "opens a new installation when it is **dispatched**". Decision B already says that "a later separately approved and otherwise admissible destructive reinstall derives 8 at its existing dispatch boundary while retaining the unknown past".

This keeps a reinstall route open after a stop. The owner decision on this bead titled "Owner decision — a late sheet that contradicts the accepted installation number" did not select Stop because it "could leave the machine with no reinstall route short of abandonment", and the one titled "Owner decision — later reinstall admission over an accepted-but-incomplete history" did not select admission B because "its only exits would be abandonment or staying in rescue". A dedicated reinstall needs a session: a reinstall approval is "bound to its reset call, entry, approved facts and the session it was rendered for", and `SEC-4` says "A typed operation that names an existing machine MUST be authorized against the calling session's binding".

Not selected:
- No ordinary session until a read shows the new id. This was the simplest option, but after a changed-label stop no session could bind, so no reinstall could be approved either.
- Bind, and have the install brief also accept the observed labels as this installation's. A changed label such as `a-9` would then have to be treated either as this installation, against changed-label A, or as foreign, which the brief treats as "the approved predecessor".
- Show the observed label as the current id. Decision B says "No label component establishes an old seed-derived identity".

Two independent readings recommended no ordinary session until a read shows the new id; the third recommended the selected option. All three called the no-session option the simplest, and all three called the policy for the stopped branches new and an amendment. One held that no ordinary session binding while the flow runs is already required by the source. None recommended accepting the observed labels as this installation's.

The readings also corrected the question as it was put to them:
- No source text reserves formatting to an approved reinstall. `STG-20` says "The label steers the model; nothing checks it", and ADR-0045 says "No label check, disk record or cross-module dependency is introduced."
- An approved destructive reinstall is not the hazard: at its dispatch a new installation opens and the old root is the predecessor erased "as approved for this install".
- The hazard is a return to rescue without a destructive reinstall. `CNF-86` exercises that return after a confirmed relabel, where it "finds one root whose label equals the shown id". Before confirmation the one root can carry another label, and neither of the brief's existing stops applies: "An unresolved label probe or two roots carrying the current id means stop and surface, never erase."
- An install unfinished in rescue is not a Resume case for Replace, which "refuses to migrate an install unfinished in rescue".

Text work named by the readings. Each holds whichever way the current text is read on the shown id in this window, either as the pending id from acceptance, since `STA-22b` says to reserve the machine index "durably before any external effect", or as no defined current id:
- A rescue-path counterpart to `STA-17`'s rule that the shown id moves "never before the disk does", which today applies "In this direct re-entry".
- A rescue-path counterpart to `STA-17`'s re-read rule, "Until a read of the label succeeds, the harness MUST re-read it on each later connection to the machine", which today follows "In that flow".
- Whether to name the rescue flow in `SEC-1`, which says "Two harness flows hold a client key outside any session", and in `SEC-5` row 1, or to fold it into Replace, a point already listed for the text work in that common-fact record.
- The install brief itself, for this window: Step 1's "An unmarked root, another installation's id or another machine's id is the predecessor, including a hand-installed root. It is erased on the selected disks as approved for this install", Step 3's "With only a predecessor, or no root, on the approved disks, partition and format as approved below" and its Resume rule, "An unmarked or foreign-id root is the approved predecessor, not a resume". The same rule is restated in ADR-0045, "an unmarked or foreign root is the predecessor, including a hand-installed one", and in `CNF-86 · BLOCKING`, "A fresh reinstall erases the approved predecessor, including an unmarked, foreign-id or hand-installed root". Each is checked against this window, in which a surfaced root is erased only once a destructive reinstall of this machine is dispatched.
- Conformance cases for the stopped branches beside `CNF-20`'s relabel cases, and an install-brief case for the surfaced root.

This record makes no normative edit and no capability, readiness or runtime claim.

## Owner decision — the command filter on a machine whose installation history is unknown, 2026-11-03

Scope: a machine recovered under decision B on this bead, where "Earlier installation history remains explicitly unknown." This answers the first open owner question in the common-fact record on this bead titled "Technical common fact — the ordinary session after a partial sheetless recovery": "Whether `ARC-25a`'s command filter applies to a machine whose earlier history is unknown under decision B." That record left it open: the filter applies "For every box-plane command targeting a machine with durable unpinned-installation history", and the record "does not decide whether unknown history counts as such history".

Selected, as a new policy and an amendment:
- On such a machine, the explicit unknown that decision B's recovery records for installation history triggers `ARC-25a`'s filter, as durable unpinned-installation history does. The filter itself is unchanged: "A match MUST prevent transmission and command-intent creation."
- The trigger is that recorded unknown and nothing broader. Absence of contrary evidence, or history that is merely incomplete, does not fire this trigger. An ordinary Restore of a sheet that carries no such recorded unknown is not caught by this trigger: its installation facts "are restored and shown beside it, as of export like the rest". Where those restored facts record an unpinned installation, the filter applies as `ARC-25a` already says, for a machine "with durable unpinned-installation history". The legacy decision on `tw-l1l`, which applies the filter to "every machine that could be the origin of the unpinned history", is unchanged.
- The filter stays on after a later pinned reinstall. Such a reinstall "opens a new installation when it is **dispatched**" (`STG-20`), and decision B already derives the next ordinal "while retaining the unknown past". A pinned successor does not resolve the unknown.
- Refusals and the trust display say unknown, never unpinned. `ARC-25a` requires one refusal "containing the target and form", and "Replay preserves the recorded refusal and its target qualification": that qualification is unknown history. What the display discloses beside the unknown history is left to the `ARC-25a` text work below. It does not assert that any installation ran unpinned.
- This decision adds no way to clear the unknown or to lift the filter. The legacy decision on `tw-l1l` left resolving the uncertainty from a matching journal backup as "a separate queued proposal, not selected by A". The queued follow-up notes after it, in the section titled "Queued follow-up notes — not decisions", warn "do not assume a match alone authorizes clearing unknown or lifting a filter". That proposal stays queued and is not extended here.

The legacy decision on `tw-l1l` (ambiguous legacy installation history, 2026-11-02) is a precedent for this tradeoff, not its authority. That decision chose to "Apply the existing ARC-25a command filter to every machine that could be the origin of the unpinned history", and accepted that "Some commands may consequently be refused on a machine that was never unpinned". It covered a backup that "preserves an unpinned predecessor on the set {M, N} but cannot identify the originating machine". There, an unpinned installation is known and only its machine is uncertain. Here, no unpinned installation is known. The technical settlement on that thread titled "Technical settlement — T47 source pruning and successor authority" limits its reach: "The explicit-unknown decision already selected for ambiguous unpinned-installation origins is not automatically extended to those other facts". Those other facts are missing legacy jump-vendor, date and account-statement data. This decision extends the filter choice to decision B's unknown installation history by owner choice, and extends nothing to those other facts.

The filter stays a narrow guard. It "does not evaluate shell or establish effective package policy", other forms "can evade the filter", and "Harmless matching text is refused". It cannot block the recovery flow itself: "No command text the harness composes contains a literal lowering form".

Not selected:
- Leaving the trigger as written, so that unknown history alone does not fire the filter. This was the simplest option. The example that separates it from the selected option is a command such as `sed -i 's/^SigLevel.*/SigLevel = Never/' /etc/pacman.conf`. Under this option it goes on to the other admissions, even though the running installation may be unpinned.
- Filtering only while the running installation's status is unknown, and lifting the filter after a recorded pinned reinstall. Lifting would end the filter while the earlier history is still unknown.

All three independent readings recommended the selected option and called leaving the trigger as written the simplest. All three called the selected option a new policy and an amendment, and none read it as already required by the source. Each reading also raised the lifting variant, and none recommended it.

The readings also corrected the question as it was put to them:
- "Missing history is never converted into empty history" is in the legacy decision on `tw-l1l`, not in decision B. Decision B's sentence is that acceptance cannot "convert a missing comparison into a passed comparison". Neither sentence forces this choice. Nor does the credential format's "Missing or invalid history MUST NOT become empty history": each governs how history and comparisons are represented, and the trigger compares nothing.
- The filter does not refuse any bytes that contain a lowering form. It works line by line: "Split raw bytes at LF." It skips comment lines: "Ignore lines whose first non-whitespace byte is `#`." A `SigLevel`-family word "followed later on that line by `=` opens a suffix through line end", in which a `Never`-family or `TrustAll`-family word selects the form.
- The question assumed a pinned running installation over an unknown past. The readings split on whether the running installation's own pin status is unknown after this recovery. One reading held that it is. Two said this cannot be told from the text, since an independent admissible record could establish it. This decision does not choose between them, and the point stays queued with the representation work below.

Text work, for the text that implements decision B:
- `ARC-25a`: the trigger, the refusal's target qualification and the display beside unknown history, including which of the disclosures it gives "Beside **unpinned**" apply there. Its package-signature disclosure describes the unpinned baseline, not a pinned reinstall.
- The recovery representation in `STA-16` and the credential format, already open in that common-fact record, which asks whether the credential format's per-machine `installation` field "needs an explicit unknown value". The trigger must key on the explicit unknown that decision B's recovery records for installation history, however that work represents it. Whether the running installation's own unrecorded status is part of that unknown is an open, unchosen question for that work.
- `SEC-14`'s restatement, under which the machine's history is shown to "every later set that includes the machine" at binding.
- Conformance cases: refusal of harmless matching text on a machine with unknown history; the filter still on after a recorded pinned reinstall; and an ordinary sheet Restore whose recorded history holds no unpinned installation and no explicit unknown, which this trigger does not catch.

This record makes no normative edit and no capability, readiness or runtime claim.

## Owner decision — a late sheet stays outside the store, 2026-11-04

Scope: the late-sheet case on this bead. A machine was recovered through the dedicated Robot rescue route under the recorded decision B, and its proposed installation number was accepted (for example, 7, with earlier history unknown). Later, the operator finds an old recovery sheet for this machine.

Selected, as an amendment of the owner's own earlier late-sheet decisions on this bead: no late-sheet act. A found sheet stays outside the store, as the enrichment record below says it does today: "no act joins a sheet's history to a store that already holds the machine". None of its facts join the live history, and none are kept for later comparison. The earlier history stays shown as unknown under the later-admission decision on this bead, and that comparison is never reported as passed.

This withdraws three owner decisions on this bead, all dated 2026-11-03, and one open point:
- "Owner decision — a valid late sheet enriches the live partial history". `STA-16` gains no late-evidence act, and the credential format gains no representation for one.
- "Owner decision — a late sheet that contradicts the accepted installation number" (decision K). Its before-write stop restated the changed-label A decision. Changed-label A is triggered by the disk's label, not by a sheet, and stands unchanged.
- "Owner decision — a refused late sheet that overlaps the admitted pin". No sheet is refused, because none is taken in. An admitted pin is governed by the existing rules alone, including `CHN-R7`'s "Without a reinstall, no installed-system pin from any source replaces an active pin".
- Whether the enrichment refusal covers the whole sheet. The enrichment record read it that way and said the owner had not confirmed it explicitly. With no enrichment there is no refusal to cover.

Unchanged: decision B; the later-admission decision; the common fact on genuine history below the accepted base, which concerns facts the harness retains at recovery, not a later sheet; the decision on an ordinary session before the rescue relabel is confirmed; and the decision on the command filter for unknown history. The ordinary-session decision cites decision K's reason for not selecting Stop. That citation records why its options were weighed and does not depend on K staying selected.

Accepted cost: the cost the enrichment record named for its own "no new act" option. A reinstall presenting a fingerprint that the found sheet records in an earlier installation is admitted, with that history shown as unknown. A found sheet that records an unpinned earlier installation does not give the machine "durable unpinned-installation history" either, so `ARC-25a`'s filter does not fire on that sheet. Whether the filter fires on the recorded unknown is the command-filter decision on this bead.

Not selected:
- Keep only the found sheet's checked fingerprints, with no merge into the live history, so that a later reinstall repeating one of them is refused.
- Keep the three withdrawn decisions as recorded.

Five independent readings judged whether the system needs the late-sheet decisions. Four recommended against keeping them as recorded: two recommended this option, and two recommended keeping only the fingerprints. The fifth recommended keeping them as recorded. The owner chose this option over the two-to-two tie, knowingly amending the owner's own earlier picks. It weakens no current text: none of the withdrawn decisions had reached the normative text.

This record makes no normative edit and no capability, readiness or runtime claim.

## Owner decision — the restart, changed-label and old-key decisions after the need review, 2026-11-04

Scope: three decisions in the record on this bead titled "Owner decision — rescue ordinal accepted as a proposal, 2026-11-02" (comment 37000001): follow-up A (the acceptance survives a worker restart), changed-label A, and old-key A. Five independent readings judged whether the system needs each of them. The owner selected the recommendation on each, as voted.

Follow-up A, the restart: the behavior stands, and the later text work adds no restart clause of its own. The durable ordinal acceptance is an ordinary journaled record under `STA-3` ("If the append fails, the transition does not occur"), bound to the same machine, root and destination allocation, and resuming the unchanged recorded migration reads it back from the journal. The limits in follow-up A stand and come from the existing rules: no revived worker authority, no different target or changed proposal, no automatic retry (`STA-6`; for the label write, `STA-17` says re-issuing it "MUST be a fresh issue the operator chooses in Replace's flow, never an automatic retry"), and no claim that a possibly sent write completed. Three readings recommended this mechanism; two recommended keeping follow-up A as recorded, with the same behavior.

Changed-label A stands as recorded: a changed label observed on the same recorded root before the relabel write stops the migration unfinished, and it adds no mandatory pre-write probe. Three readings recommended keeping it as recorded. Two recommended simplifying it: one by merging it with the late-sheet conflict rules, which the late-sheet decision on this bead (comment 72000001) has since withdrawn, and one by a compare-and-set inside the relabel job. Neither simplification is selected.

Old-key A stands as recorded: only the exact old public key that checked retained machine records identify is removed, after the new-key login and the confirmed `b-7` readback; unknown keys stay untouched and revocation is reported incomplete. Four readings recommended keeping it as recorded. One recommended rewriting `authorized_keys` to the new key alone after the login and readback; that whole-file option stays queued and unchosen, as old-key A recorded it.

Open for the later text work: when the old key cannot be identified, old-key A leaves it in place, and BLOCKING `CNF-5` reads "only that machine's public key appears in its `authorized_keys`". The text work must reconcile old-key A with `CNF-5` and must not weaken `CNF-5` to do so. `STA-17`'s direct Replace already leaves an old key in place on a failed confirmation ("a failed confirmation leaves the old key in place") and never reports complete revocation while it remains outstanding. This record does not choose how the two are reconciled.

Unchanged: decision B, job-order A, the later-admission decision, the ordinary-session decision, and the late-sheet decision.

This record makes no normative edit and no capability, readiness or runtime claim.

comments.text:
## Agent Brief — bounded specification amendment, the dedicated rescue rekey's ordinal, relabel and partial history

**Category:** bug. **Outcome:** land, in their normative homes, the owner decisions and technical common facts already recorded on this bead. No further owner choice is needed for the scope below. Points the owner left unchosen stay unchosen: where the text work would have to choose one, stop and report it instead of choosing. The bead moves to ready-for-agent with this brief; the drain lane takes it after its current queue.

This bead's description is the question as filed, and it says the gap must be settled before a dedicated-server path is offered, "which no stage before the third does". Stages are removed (tw-o6r). The governing admission row is "The dedicated path: the construction test bed" in `07-conformance.md`, whose cases, item 84's Robot rescue case and item 20's relabel cases included, pass on the integrated harness "before a dedicated-server path is offered to an operator". This brief governs the text work.

**Records this brief implements (sections on this bead, by title).** Each section's own text, limits and "Not selected" list govern. This brief summarizes them and widens none.

- "Owner decision — rescue ordinal accepted as a proposal, 2026-11-02" (decision B), with its follow-up A, job-order A, display timing, changed-label A and old-key A.
- "Owner decision — later reinstall admission over an accepted-but-incomplete history, 2026-11-03" (admission A).
- "Technical common fact — genuine history below the accepted base is kept, 2026-11-03".
- "Technical common fact — the ordinary session after a partial sheetless recovery, 2026-11-03". Both of its open owner questions are closed: the second by the ordinary-session decision below, the first by the filter removal ("Scope of the filter withdrawal, 2026-11-04").
- "Owner decision — an ordinary session before the rescue relabel is confirmed, 2026-11-03".
- "Owner decision — the command filter on a machine whose installation history is unknown, 2026-11-03", only the points that "Scope of the filter withdrawal, 2026-11-04" keeps standing.
- "Owner decision — a late sheet stays outside the store, 2026-11-04".
- "Owner decision — the restart, changed-label and old-key decisions after the need review, 2026-11-04".

Withdrawn, and implemented by none of this brief: the three late-sheet decisions of 2026-11-03 ("Owner decision — a valid late sheet enriches the live partial history", "Owner decision — a late sheet that contradicts the accepted installation number" (K) and "Owner decision — a refused late sheet that overlaps the admitted pin"), withdrawn by the 2026-11-04 late-sheet decision; and the filter parts of the command-filter decision (its trigger, the filter staying on after a pinned reinstall, the refusal's target qualification and its conformance cases), withdrawn by "Owner direction — the command filter is removed, and C8 is moot, 2026-11-04" as scoped by "Scope of the filter withdrawal, 2026-11-04".

**Current gap.** `STA-17`'s relabel applies "In this direct re-entry", and `ARC-43`'s `replace_root_label` runs "during Replace's model-free direct re-entry migration". The rescue recovery that `STA-22b` describes moves the machine to a fresh-seed index with no relabel, no defined ordinal `n` and no rule for when the machine counts as migrated. No representation carries a history whose earlier installations are unknown, and the credential format says "Missing or invalid history MUST NOT become empty history". `STG-20`'s reinstall admission "MUST share no fingerprint with any observation or installed-system pin of that machine in any earlier installation", which such a history cannot show. The install brief treats a root whose label differs from the shown id as the predecessor, so a return to rescue before confirmation can steer toward erasing the machine's own root.

**Desired behavior and owners.** Normative owners are `STA-17`, `STG-20`, `STA-16` and the credential format, with `ARC-43` for the job and the install brief for the surfaced root; decision B places the rationale with ADR-0045. Change the single owners together, then record the amendment.

- **The ordinal, decision B**, at `STA-17` and `STG-20`. During authorized rescue recovery of the same physical maintained machine, with no admissible saved history and a unique disk label such as `a-7`, the operator may explicitly accept 7 as a proposed current installation ordinal after checks against surviving facts; migration to new index b uses `b-7`. A disk label is never adopted automatically, and no label component establishes an old seed-derived identity. The number is a proposal, never historical proof. Earlier history stays explicitly unknown; known history carries forward; every retained identity, ordinal, observation and pin fact is preserved. Acceptance cannot override a contradiction or turn a missing comparison into a passed one. Reading or accepting a label opens no destructive installation, establishes no prior pin provenance, authenticates no root contents, identifies no old client key, revokes nothing and completes no Replace. The base does not increment during non-destructive recovery; a later separately approved, otherwise admissible destructive reinstall derives 8 at its existing dispatch boundary, retaining the unknown past and waiving no guard.
- **The partial-history representation**, at the credential format (a new version) and `STA-16`. It round-trips the proposal's basis and the missing past without turning either into ordinary recovered history. Old-version validation is unchanged, its refusal of a "duplicate or skipped installation ordinal" included; fabricate no earlier groups, observations, pins or empty-history placeholders. The compact export carries its own interpretable acceptance basis and unknown-history meaning; a pointer to missing journal evidence is not enough. Genuine admissible facts below the accepted base are preserved, with the gaps around them shown as unknown. Keep the captured observation and root provenance, the target-bound operator act, retained facts, relabel intent and result, and captured confirmation as separate linked facts. A failed acceptance append supplies no acceptance. The representation supplies no authority for later operations. No field names are chosen.
- **Restart.** The acceptance is an ordinary journaled record under `STA-3` ("If the append fails, the transition does not occur"), bound to the same machine, root and destination allocation; resuming the unchanged recorded migration reads it back. Add no restart clause of its own. Its limits come from existing rules: no revived worker authority, no different target or changed proposal, no automatic retry (`STA-6`, and `STA-17`'s "MUST be a fresh issue the operator chooses in Replace's flow, never an automatic retry"), and no claim that a possibly sent write completed.
- **The job and its order, job-order A**, at `STA-17` and `ARC-43`'s job list, which today has no rescue rekey job. Write the root label and read it back only after the installed system accepts a login authenticated with the new client key. The bounded harness job runs in the installed system. A failed new-key login leaves `a-7` untouched. A pinned host answer or rescue authentication is not installed-system acceptance of the key. Keep the relabel's captured readback distinct from installed access, old-key revocation and whole Replace completion. Give the rescue path counterparts of `STA-17`'s "never before the disk does" and of "Until a read of the label succeeds, the harness MUST re-read it on each later connection to the machine".
- **Display.** After acceptance, show `b-7` as the proposed or pending destination, and distinguish allocation `b`, observed disk text `a-7`, installed access and label confirmation. Confirmed label and current-id status need the captured installed-system readback after the new-key login. Once a write is sent, the observed `a-7` is only an as-of observation. Label confirmation, terminal job evidence, hold release and revocation stay separate facts.
- **A changed label, changed-label A.** If an admissible captured observation of the same recorded root reports a changed label (such as `a-9`) before the relabel write, stop this bounded migration unfinished and preserve the discrepancy. Issue no relabel intent or write. Retain the acceptance, both observations, the allocation and every association under 7; adopt no 9 and invent no installation boundary. The earlier new-key installation is not undone. The stop creates no command hold without a sent command, grants no erasure and implies no cleanup or revocation. Add no mandatory pre-write probe. Restart does not normalize the discrepancy into success.
- **The old key, old-key A.** The model-free flow removes only the exact old client public key that checked retained machine records for the same authorized machine identify, after the installed-system new-key login and the confirmed `b-7` readback. Preserve the new key and unrelated authorizations. Missing old private material is not missing public identity; report no impossible old-key login test as passed. Unknown keys stay untouched and revocation is reported incomplete; they supply no deletion target, no whole-file replacement and no new command hold. A removal supports only its scoped effect. The changed-label stop does not proceed to removal.
- **Later reinstall admission, admission A**, at `STG-20`, for this dedicated Robot recovery path only. A later `ready_to_reset` pin is compared against every fact the harness retains, retained facts below the accepted base included; any known overlap refuses. The earlier history is shown as unknown, and that comparison is never reported, displayed or exported as passed. The guard does not refuse merely because earlier facts are unavailable. title: Define the single-machine session route to a different entry after definitive failure
description:
# Define the single-machine session route to a different entry after definitive failure

## Question

When the sole machine allocation of a stage-1 session definitively fails, can that same live session order a different newly approved entry? How is that consistent with retained bound-set membership and the single-machine stage-1 constraint? If it needs a successor session, what ends the old one and authorizes the new one?

## Established boundary

SEC-1 says "No machine leaves a set while the session is alive — what the model has read from it stays in the context that commands the rest."

STA-24 says "A different approved entry is independent, and creating it while a sibling is unresolved is permitted under its own approval, whose card shows the unresolved sibling and that it may be billing."

The unresolved-sibling rule supplies neither an exception to session membership nor an automatic route after definitive failure. A different entry and a new allocation index are not themselves authority to grow or shrink a single-machine session. The pending bounded repair adds no such route.

## Answer must demonstrate

- Specify the permissible stage-1 route, including old session membership, any required session end/successor, approval of the new entry and retained failed-allocation history.
- Distinguish same-entry replacement from a different entry, unresolved sibling from definitive failure, and stage-1 single-machine sessions from stage-2 set growth. Preserve any profile independence-bound constraint.
- Supply conformance refusal for an unauthorized added entry and admission for the chosen operator-approved route; a fresh index must not bypass the boundary.
- Land the answer with SEC-1/ARC-15 and the stage-1 applicability owners, updating affected formalized clauses and prose together.

No live vendor call or runtime reproduction is claimed. This is a specification question, not an implementation instruction to add automatic retries or discard a failed member.

Category: bug. State: needs-triage. Priority: P2. No behavior answer, implementation readiness or closure is implied by filing this question.
close_reason: Landed: a different approved entry replaces a never-sent machine entry in the same session, marking Failed in the same sole-writer act (STA-22b; SEC-1, SEC-4, ARC-15, STA-24, CNF-72, ADR-0037 amendment; PR #80)

The selected case includes an order proven never sent while an earlier preparation step has unknown outcome. That preparation remains unresolved and restricted; this decision supplies no failure, success, non-execution, cancellation or deletion evidence for it. A genuinely independent replacement does not reuse or repeat the uncertain preparation under another label. Every applicable identity exclusion and independent guard still applies to the replacement, including an exclusion originating from the old entry.

Coordinate with tw-hwl: a fresh allocation/index/account/cost for the same intended entry uses its separately selected same-entry route. This decision supplies the distinct, explicitly approved replacement-entry act within the same unfinished setup and live session. A new account/index/call, renaming the old entry or merely displaying it as historical is not replacement authority.

The amendment must atomically retire old prospective authorization and queued authority before admitting the new entry. It must retain old records and restrictions without authorizing another command/order on the retired entry through a stale approval or late completion. This local-only act removes no actual bound machine and grants no stage-1 larger set. ## Owner decision — what makes a replacement a different intended entry, 2026-11-05

The replacement act in `STA-22b` refuses a replacement that "differs from the old entry only in its approved-entry identity, label, allocation, index, account, cost or call, which makes it the same intended entry". The question was what, beyond that list, makes a replacement a different intended entry. For example: same vendor and plan with a different region, or the same region with a different size or image.

The owner picked "Changes to the machine count". A replacement whose vendor, plan or size, region or image differs from the old entry's is a different intended entry, and the act may admit it if every other refusal clears. A replacement that differs only in its bundle commit, or in an incidental argument such as an order's reference field, together with the listed facts, is still the same intended entry. The same intended entry still has no successor.

**The counts.** Four independent readers were asked. On whether the text already forces an answer, three said it does not decide and one said it forces this reading. On the recommendation, three backed this reading and one backed a test of the entry's role or purpose. In its first wording the option took in "other approved create facts", and one reader noted that this was too broad because it covered the bundle commit and the reference field. The pick uses the narrowed wording.

**Framing corrections the text work keeps:** `STA-24`'s barrier ("While any call naming a resource is unresolved") is not what holds back the same intended entry; the refusal is `STA-22b`'s own clause (two of four). This pick decides only whether an entry is distinct. Every other refusal of the act still applies, including "when the replacement would reuse or repeat an unresolved preparation step of the old entry". Whether a step of the same kind under the replacement's new identity (for example `STG-21`'s email submission) counts as such a repeat is a separate point, not decided here (three of four readers said the text cannot tell).

**Not selected:** requiring a change of the entry's role or purpose.

Neither option weakens `STA-24`'s barrier, `CNF-72` or a theorem ("The formal companion has no replacement act"). The text lands with `STA-22b` and `ARC-15`, with `CNF-72` cases for an admitted region, size or image change and a refused bundle-commit-only change.

This owner decision is settled and must not be re-asked. It makes no normative edit and no capability, readiness or runtime claim.

No theorem changes: "The formal companion has no replacement act".

title: What does the sheet hold for an old public key still awaiting removal after migration?
description:
## Why this issue exists

Found while settling `tw-rds` (comment 115000001). The credential format's version-7 text says "A migrated machine has no entry", and `STA-17` says of a dedicated machine's relabel "only after that may the old key be removed". So after an ordinary migration the machine's entry and records move to the new seed in one journal act, while its retired-seed public key is still installed and awaits removal. Nothing on the new seed's sheet records that old key. After a Restore from that sheet, the harness cannot tell that a retired public key is still on the machine or finish its removal.

The `tw-rds` pick has the same shape for a superseded reservation: the act that migrates the machine ends the reservation's entry, though its recorded key is "one more retired public key that re-entry removes".

## Question

What does the sheet hold for a migrated machine's old public key, and a superseded reservation's, until re-entry removes it? Whether this needs a sheet record, a screen statement or nothing is a real choice; the text does not force it.

## Closes when

The credential format's payload version 7 (or a later version), `STA-17` and `CNF-84` say what the sheet holds for a retired public key still installed after its machine migrated, and what a Restore from that sheet does with it, without weakening `STA-22b`'s derive-and-compare check or any existing theorem, gate, requirement or assumption.

comments.text: Scope, from the tw-rds review pass (2026-11-05): the same gap covers the read-confirmed branch of a later Replace. After a failed relabel read the machine's original retired-seed key stays installed; when the next Replace's label read shows the reserved index's id, one act confirms that migration and ends the machine's original entry, and nothing on the sheet then records that original key, whose removal is still owed. A fix may require removal before the last tracking entry ends, keep a pending entry until removal is confirmed, or state the limit on the screen; the text does not force one.

title: Under an untyped vendor scope, does a destructive hold refuse harness-started jobs?
description:
`STA-24` pauses "a box-plane command to any machine of the session's bound set at that vendor" while a call under the scope is open or unresolved, and says "a continuation that continues ends the pause and a destructive one does not (*the hold*, below)"; the hold "keeps the model's box-plane commands to the machines of the session's bound set at that vendor stopped until the operator replaces it". Whether a harness-composed job (`digest_secret`, `delivery_reboot`, `replace_root_label`) is refused under the hold is unsettled, and ADR-0050 stops every box-plane job "whoever starts it" for a machine's destructive disposition.

ADR-0038 records: "Abandonment still has no typed destroy to run at such a vendor, and `ARC-21` and `ARC-22` now hand the act to the operator; while a disposition naming abandonment or a destructive reinstall stands on the scope, `STA-24` holds every further call under it and the model's box-plane commands to the set's machines at that vendor until the operator replaces the disposition (ADR-0044)."
close_reason: Specified that under an untyped vendor scope a destructive disposition's hold refuses every new box-plane job to a machine it covers, whoever starts it (STA-24), with coverage anchored on the approving session's bound set and its lawful growth up to its final recorded reach. The destructive hold carries by exact origin to a later untyped scope's calls only, and an unresolved call is inherited at the same exact origin under a changed credential; neither carries by vendor identity across origins. SEC-4 closes local permission when its session ends, and resupplying the credential or accepting the mode alone carries no permission over. A successor keeps the pause on the same covered machine under the same credential; the pause's other succession edges stay open in T47. CNF-105 gains the discriminating cases, a destructive replacement stays a hold, and ARC-15, SEC-14, STA-23, T47 and ADR-0038/0044/0050 point to the owners. ADR-0054 records it. Specified, not enabled; runtime remains outstanding.

All three independent readings picked A and called it simplest. Two called it an amendment resolving the reserved lifetime policy; the third called it a source-forced clarification. Record the explicit owner resolution with that classification disagreement intact. Agreement about the preferred behavior was not permission to self-settle a disputed amendment.

The strongest arguments were a clear authority boundary without orphaned exclusivity; current-session approval with exposure history retained; and the risk that persistent exclusivity otherwise blocks successor entry. The last argument favored A but did not establish that every explicit-close or transfer alternative was impossible.

The alternatives not selected were B, reuse historical permission after the successor's fresh mode acceptance, including automatic transfer; C, keep local permission and exclusivity until explicit local closure, then approve anew; and D, explicit successor adoption of the historical permission. An adoption that itself authorizes successor calls is substantively a fresh local approval. Also considered and rejected were E, permission remaining attached to the ended session; F, timer expiry; and G, expiry on ordinary hide. Ordinary hide remains distinct from actual end. Attribution is not reproduced here.

Local permission closure does not establish external credential revocation, erase history or end disclosure of a still-exposed credential. Retained calls and standing dispositions keep their records. The separately selected unresolved-call inheritance A and destructive-call inheritance B are unchanged; fresh approval does not evade either. No new raw-secret custody, account-proof mechanism or permission transfer protocol is selected.

Closing the old local exclusivity removes that particular obstacle to successor binding. It does not grant binding authority or waive current origin/vendor-identity, known-machine, independence, capability or other admissions. The owner separately selected successor-job applicability A in the section “Owner decision — successor-job applicability of the destructive hold, 2026-11-03” on this bead. Closing local permission did not itself decide that machine-job policy.

## Source quotations and owning work

STA-23 says "Individual session end destroys that session's runtime authority and pending approvals; it does not revive on return."

SEC-4 says "The scope MUST be refused if any undestroyed machine provisioned through that origin, or through that vendor identity, lies outside the calling session's bound set; and while the scope stands, no such machine is bound to another session."

ARC-15 says "No untyped call runs before its scope is approved."

SEC-14 says "A mode is accepted by the session that does what it governs, before doing it."

ADR-0017 says "closing the approval stops new calls, but it does not invalidate a bearer key the service has seen".

Specify the selected local permission/exclusivity lifetime at SEC-4, coordinating ARC-15, SEC-14, STA-23 and the T47 reservation without duplicating the rule. Retain stage-2 conformance for actual end, lawful successor approval/acceptance, ordinary hide, continuing external exposure and inherited call restrictions. Existing formal results are not evidence that this untyped-scope lifetime policy is implemented.

This is a decision record, not a normative edit, readiness or closure claim.

## Owner decision — successor-job applicability of the destructive hold, 2026-11-03

Selected A: a successor's new jobs stay held on the originally covered machines until the operator replaces the destructive disposition. This covers the original set's lawful later growth up to its final recorded reach, but does not cover the successor's unrelated machines. The hold applies to every new box-plane job within that reach, whoever starts it, preserving the earlier all-new-jobs decision.

All three independent readings picked A and called it simplest. Two called successor applicability a clarification; the third called it an amendment requiring an explicit successor-job admission rule. Record the owner resolution with that disagreement intact. The strongest arguments were that the specified release had never occurred; that a session end must not bypass the standing destructive choice; and that Lock followed by re-entry must not stand in for the chosen wipe.

Unchosen alternatives were B, end job applicability with the old session; C, freeze coverage at the time the disposition was recorded; D, hold the successor's whole set at that vendor; E, carry the hold only if the successor also approves another vendor scope; and F, refuse successor binding until replacement. All readings rejected B as a bypass, although one called it mechanically short. C loses lawful later original-set growth; D broadens coverage to unrelated machines; E permits a successor without a new vendor scope to evade the job hold; F adds a binding refusal. Attribution is not reproduced here. None is selected by A.

The old disposition and scope retain their identity and history. A successor need not approve a new vendor scope for the original machine-job restriction to apply. Closing the predecessor's local scope permission/exclusivity under the separately selected lifetime A is not replacement of its destructive disposition. The unresolved-call A and destructive-call B decisions remain unchanged. Binding, capability and other admissions remain independent; this decision grants no new successor authority.

Existing-record collection and local paste retain their separate guards. A newly dispatched read, digest or reboot is a new job rather than collection of an existing record. Replacing the disposition releases this restriction subject to all other admissions; no automatic retry, operation-success inference or retrospective settlement is selected.

This closes the remaining scope/session-succession decisions for tw-pgp. It does not implement the amendments or establish runtime conformance. The disputed historical post-erasure proof remains unendorsed; the selected exact-origin call rule supplies the call result without that proof.

## Source quotations and owning work

STA-24 says "a disposed call is not an open one."

STA-24 says "doing so releases nothing by itself, and the replacement does."

STA-24 says "Machines outside the bound set, or at another vendor, are not held by this".

SEC-1 says "A set grows by one operator act per machine, and never shrinks while its session lives."

STA-20 says "Collection MUST remain an available fresh privileged read of the existing record, including while ordinary commands and harness jobs are held."

Specify successor-job applicability at STA-24, keeping original reach and the existing replacement release, coordinated with the other selected tw-pgp decisions and ADR-0044/0050. Retain stage-2 refusal coverage for successor model and harness jobs, including a successor without a later vendor scope, lawful original-set growth, and positive boundaries for unrelated machines, existing-record collection and valid disposition replacement. Existing formal results do not prove this untyped job-hold policy.

This is a decision record, not a normative edit or a closure/readiness claim for implementation.

The records read "actual session end" against the session rules of 2026-11-03. tw-l1l's "Owner decision — sessions survive every local event until End, 2026-11-04" (comment 69000001) has since changed which events end a session: no local event does, and an explicit Lock is not one. **Current gap.** `STA-24`'s hold "keeps the model's box-plane commands to the machines of the session's bound set at that vendor stopped until the operator replaces it". It names model commands only, so a harness-started job is unsettled. `STA-24`'s inheritance covers only "A scope re-approved for the same origin and credential", and ADR-0038 says "a token rotated at the same origin starts with no unresolved barrier". No text says when the local scope permission closes, or whether the hold reaches a successor's jobs. No current Dispatch theorem carries the untyped pause or hold.

**Desired behavior and owners:**

- **All new jobs are held** (35000001), at `STA-24`, recorded as an amendment, not as what the model-only wording already meant. While the destructive disposition stands, every new box-plane job within the covered vendor and bound-set reach is held, whoever starts it. That includes model commands, digest, reboot, delivery-check read, relabel and key-migration jobs. A freshly issued read job is a new command. Collection of an existing record stays available (`STA-20`: "Collection MUST remain an available fresh privileged read of the existing record, including while ordinary commands and harness jobs are held."), and so does the local paste, which sends nothing to the machine and neither clears the hold nor authorizes a job. The release stays the operator's replacement of the disposition: "doing so releases nothing by itself, and the replacement does." The new hold overrides no deletion, pin, binding, command-hold or custody requirement, and it creates no new recovery sweep or protection for journal-omitted work. None of these is the replacement: manual vendor work or its report, late observations, key replacement, a new token or approval, local buffer clearing, a Lock, or actual session end. A true service revocation ends that credential's external authority but proves no deletion or operation success, and it is not the replacement either.
- **Destructive-call inheritance** (B), at `STA-24`. A standing destructive hold carries to every later scope at the same exact origin after token rotation or reapproval. Calls through that later scope are refused, regardless of credential equality, approval id or overlap with the held machines. A fresh eligible session does not bypass it by approving a later scope at that origin. This is exact-origin inheritance, not vendor-identity inheritance across origins. Inheritance supplies no approval or binding authority. The original disposition and its calls keep their identities and resource, with no journal rewrite or synthetic settlement.
- **Unresolved-call inheritance** (A), at `STA-24`, amending its sentence "A scope re-approved for the same origin and credential inherits the outstanding call". Update ADR-0038's "a token rotated at the same origin starts with no unresolved barrier" to match. After a credential change, every later untyped scope at the same exact origin inherits the unresolved call, with no credential comparison. Accepted cost: a different account at the same origin is blocked until the original call has a valid terminal record. Same-origin, same-credential inheritance stays mandatory. Session end, credential erasure, reapproval and manual vendor work are not terminal reconciliation. A valid terminal record ends the barrier. A destructive disposition then engages B, and a continuing one creates no hold.
- **Local permission lifetime** (A), at `SEC-4`, coordinated with `ARC-15`, `SEC-14`, `STA-23` and the T47 record without duplicating the rule. At actual session end the local scope permission and its exclusivity close. The successor approves afresh, on the card where it accepts the mode, and one card act may both approve and accept. Resupplying a credential or accepting the mode alone carries no permission over. Closing permission is not external revocation, erases no history and ends no disclosure of a still-exposed credential.
- **Successor-job applicability** (A), at `STA-24`, coordinated with ADR-0044 and ADR-0050. A successor's new jobs stay held on the originally covered machines until the replacement, including the original set's lawful later growth up to its final recorded reach. The successor's unrelated machines are not held. The successor needs no new vendor scope for the hold to apply. Closing the predecessor's local permission is not the replacement.
- **Settled boundaries** (46000001 and the residual review): no token fingerprint, credential-derived durable reference, account proof or runtime framework. Known-machine exclusivity is checked independently, and a new token does not evade it. No untyped call becomes a typed read by its name. Machines outside the bound set, or at another vendor, stay unaffected.
- **Records to coordinate after the rules change:** `CNF-105`, the T47 record, and ADR-0038, ADR-0044 and ADR-0050's references.

**Stop and report — choose none of these:**

- Manual vendor-work recording and non-vendor scopes. Both stay queued separately.
- Any credential-recognition mechanism, and the disputed historical claim that the former same-credential text already forced refusal after erasure. The selected exact-origin rule gives the call result without it.
- Proposals not selected:
  - for the calls (B): A, origin plus overlap; C, new scopes separate; D, same-credential only; E, an operator predecessor link; F, verified-account lineage; G, refusing the new scope approval; H, vendor-identity carry across origins;
  - for unresolved calls (A): B, keep the same-credential boundary; C, allow the call and show the outstanding one; D, operator linkage; E, refusing the new approval; F, overlap only;
  - for permission lifetime (A): B, reuse after fresh acceptance or automatic transfer; C, keep until explicit close; D, explicit adoption; E, attached to the ended session; F, a timer; G, expiry on hide;
  - for successor jobs (A): B, ending with the old session; C, freezing coverage at the disposition; D, the successor's whole set at that vendor; E, only with another vendor scope; F, refusing successor binding.
- Any edit that would weaken a theorem, gate, assumption boundary or requirement beyond what a named decision qualifies, or enable an untyped scope. Stop and report the conflict.

**Acceptance criteria:**

Where a touched clause is formalized, change its Lean declaration and its prose together. Existing theorems supply no evidence for these untyped rules; do not cite them as such.

## Owner decision — deletion, retired references and held output, 2026-11-02

Selected A: confirmed deletion of M ends M's placed-secret scan reference and M's unarmed-reference wait. Bytes withheld before that deletion remain withheld: deletion never counts as a scan. Output produced after deletion is no longer checked for M's value, and the display states that limit. No peer-reference lifetime extension or release of the old withheld backlog is selected.

SEC-5 states: "Exact copies of a placed secret whose reference the browser holds are redacted from box-plane output before that output reaches the model or the transcript, and the claim is no wider than that." Its coverage limit is "It covers only placements whose reference the browser holds". Row 23 removes the persistent comparison material on destruction. Preserve those boundaries and "Unscanned bytes MUST be withheld": no old range becomes scanned, safe or releasable because a reference retired. Fresh output still owes every other applicable scan and release prerequisite.

Use stable record or range identity to retain the old withholding decision across later collection. The same pre-deletion job output range cannot pass as new output because it is re-collected, replayed, re-requested, displayed after deletion or assigned a later retrieval time. A range whose eligibility as post-deletion production is not established cannot be promoted to new output merely because its collection is late. This calls for protected non-secret identity and classification, not retention or export of raw application values, bare digests or expired scan material.

Retiring M's unarmed-reference wait lifts only that reference prerequisite. It clears no command hold, resource barrier, pending check, other unarmed-reference requirement, destructive restriction or unknown command outcome; it does not shrink an actual session's membership or authorize new contact with a deleted machine. A stop, renewal-off, deletion date, reinstall or disposition is not this deletion boundary. Use the admitted durably recorded deletion confirmation, with its existing evidence limits, rather than claiming irreversible physical erasure or revocation of the credential at its service.

The normative amendment belongs in SEC-5's scan/lifetime transition and ARC-43's required-reference/release rule, with SEC-6's coverage display and CNF-95(e/f) coordinated after the rules change. Add a targeted control that releases a pre-deletion unscanned backlog after deletion and require the CNF-95 finding. Include recollection of that same old range as a refusal and useful fresh-output admission after the selected boundary, subject to the remaining active references. Preserve cross-chunk matching for all references still required.

Peer-output effects are stage 2; this decision admits no larger set or new capability and supplies no runtime evidence. It changes neither service revocation policy nor tw-i55's human part. title: Decide retired-seed handoffs and a pending migration index at a later Replace
description:
tw-1wq's text (ADR-0058) leaves two retired-seed points open, both named in the credential format's payload version 7.

**Handoffs.** The format says "What the new seed's sheet holds for a handoff allocated under a retired seed is not yet specified". `retired_allocations` admits only the families `machine` and `pass`, and `STA-22b`'s journal-keep list names no handoff.

**A pending migration index at a later Replace.** The format says "neither is what a later Replace does with a `migration_index` whose reserved allocation is under the seed that Replace retires". A `migration_index` must name a machine allocation in the current `allocations`. After a failed relabel read the machine keeps its retired-seed name and its new index stays reserved; a second Replace retires the seed that reservation was made under, so the export has no current allocation to name. `STA-17`'s direct re-entry ("a dedicated machine counts as migrated only when a read shows the new id") and the reserved key that may already be on the machine both bear on it. A Failed tombstone does not fit: `STA-22b` says "Failed requires local proof that this allocation's create was never sent".

Until both are written, a Replace export in either case can fail its own import (`CNF-84`: "no export can write a sheet its own import refuses").

**Handoffs: keep it under its retired seed.** The new seed's sheet carries each handoff the journal keeps under a retired seed in `retired_allocations`, family `handoff`, with its seed, index, tenant and handoff ID, recorded public key and `outstanding` with a closed reason, for as long as its declared lifetime runs. The post-harness machinery is given the credential only after the harness derives it from the retired seed the operator supplies and compares it with the recorded key. Using it is a step that needs the retired seed, so Replace's screen says the retired seed stays needed for it. The entry ends in one journal act when the journal records the profile's declared end. Replace does not re-issue a handoff: its public half is installed only during setup, over the bound session's channel, and a sealed machine cannot be told a new key.

**Pending migration index: read first, else supersede it.** When a later Replace re-enters a machine whose migration index is under the seed that Replace retires, it first takes the label read `STA-17` already requires. A read showing the reserved index's id confirms that migration in one journal act, and the machine then migrates like any machine of that seed. Otherwise the machine keeps its own retired-seed entry and gets a fresh migration index under the new seed, and the old reservation becomes its own retired machine entry: `outstanding` with reason `"superseded_reservation"`, linked to the machine's entry. Like a migration index, it is not a second machine: no record names it, and it has no machine state or artifact history. Its recorded key is one more retired public key that re-entry removes from the machine. The act that migrates or destroys the machine also ends its superseded reservations. A third Replace copies them unchanged.

The text forces neither part: four of four. It does exclude two options. Re-issuing a handoff under the new seed conflicts with "during setup, before the handoff point" and "over the bound session's own channel". Dropping the reservation conflicts with "Failed requires local proof that this allocation's create was never sent", given the reserved key was installed. Once a read shows the reserved id, `STA-17`'s "A later read showing the new id confirms the relabel without another write" decides that branch.

**What these picks widen or amend, named:**

- 113000001's "`retired_allocations` carrying every allocation the journal keeps under an earlier seed" covers handoffs too, beyond machine and pass entries; the recorded-key acceptance, deferred to before use, covers a retired handoff.
- `STA-17`'s "needs its backup *during* Replace and abandons it after" and `SEC-5` row 15's "until the last step that needs it is done": a retired-seed handoff's use, while its lifetime runs, is such a step.
- 113000001's "the reserved index is linked, not a second machine" gains a second linked kind, the superseded reservation; the format's "the one repeated mapping import accepts" widens to it.
- `CNF-84` (BLOCKING): import accepts family `handoff`, the new machine reason and the link member, and refuses their malformed forms.

**Not selected:** for handoffs, re-issuing under the new seed where a channel remains, and ending the handoff at Replace; for the pending index, re-entering without the read, and dropping the reservation.

**Version.** This amends payload version 7, as 113000001 did; its text marks both points not yet specified, and nothing in the repository writes a version-7 sheet.

**What the text work must write in:** the credential format's version-7 text (family, handoff reason, superseded reservation and link, import checks, exporter rule); `STA-22b`'s keep list; `STA-17`'s Replace export paragraph and backup sentence; `SEC-5` row 15; `CNF-84`; ADR-0058's open points, closed by a new ADR.

This owner decision is settled and must not be re-asked. It makes no normative edit by itself and no capability, readiness or runtime claim.

- Run the unpiped Nix check-all gate before/after, CI's offline unit suite and full discriminating mutation controls, with actual exits and preserved limitations.

**Out of scope:** Same-entry or different-entry successor authority (tw-hwl/tw-nj8), live-session substitution policy, post-send negative vendor evidence or its audit, installation target/acceptance (tw-l1l), runtime code in this repository, any new capability admission or gate/theorem weakening. The existing supported abandonment-before-order route remains available; merely supporting this bounded terminal transition does not create an email-verification recovery mechanism.

title: Decide whether the LNVPS recovery row owes CNF evidence for the deletion reader's Replace half
description:
The LNVPS path's recovery row in `07-conformance.md` ("The LNVPS path: recovery export/import and Replace") requires the Replace cases before maintained-cloud delivery. It also says the dedicated, model-free deletion reader (`tw-ae7` comment 60000001) is specified, and that its scope over the old machine of an LNVPS Replace rebuild applies wherever LNVPS Replace is offered. No CNF item names the reader, so nothing in that row requires evidence of the reader's Replace half.

## Question

Is integrated evidence of the reader's Replace half owed before LNVPS Replace is offered, and if so, which CNF item carries it (a case in an existing recovery item, or a new item with its row)?

## Bounds

- Raised during the stage removal (`tw-o6r`) and deliberately kept out of that edit.
- Do not narrow or widen the recovery row in the meantime. The reader's unfinished-setup half stays with the in-setup replacement order's row ("Before enabling the in-setup replacement order at LNVPS"), which reads "none yet".
- Whether "unfinished setup" covers an abandoned setup still waiting on M's deletion is a separate open question; this bead does not answer it.
- Related: `tw-ae7` comments 60000001 and 68000001.
close_reason: Landed decision 91000001 in 07-conformance.md: CNF-20 gains the deletion check's Replace-use case and CNF-26 its abandonment-use case, each with scope, no-automatic-start, no-key and no-session/SSH-key/model refusals. The recovery row requires CNF-20's case before the check is offered for a machine Replace's flow stopped, and the LNVPS delivery row requires CNF-26's case before it is offered for a machine the abandonment flow stopped; each use is gated by its own case, the in-setup rung's machine stays with the in-setup order's row, and neither case is required before delivery. T44's gate is kept. Specified, not enabled; runtime remains outstanding.

title: Does anything hold a restored machine whose pre-loss command may still be running?
description:
## Decision — journal-only, 2026-11-01

The owner chose journal-only protection. Add no recovery check or hold for commands absent from the restored journal. New work after recovery, including Replace's model-free key migration, may overlap an earlier command the restored journal does not record. Intents without terminal records that a backup does retain still hold under the existing journal-derived rules. Other admission checks and standing restrictions remain in force.

## Why this issue exists

A machine can keep running a command after the phone loses the journal that recorded its send. A sheet contains no outstanding-call record. An imported local-store backup differs from total journal loss: it may retain some unresolved intents, while omitting later sends. The original question's claim that nothing journaled holds every restored machine was too broad for that backup case.

`STA-24` states "The barrier is a fact of the journal — an intent with no terminal record" and "What this rule cannot reach is a journal that is lost with the phone: `STA-14` states that transcripts are gone, and a recovery sheet is not an outstanding-call record." `STA-20` records jobs "on persistent disk (`/var/lib/tau-web/jobs`, root-only)" and says "On the installed system the files survive a reboot". Those surviving machine records do not recreate a lost journal intent.

`STA-21` states "The job record is machine-reported and advisory." Enumeration cannot reveal commands that left no record, prove completeness against a hostile machine or reconstruct approvals. This limit must not be presented as a new concurrency guarantee.

## Triage outcome

Astra and Sol recommended a bounded recovery guard. Opus recommended an operator-cancellable advisory wait. Fable was a missing seat because of its usage limit; Grok was a missing seat because of HTTP 402 balance exhaustion. The owner explicitly rejected those recommendations in favor of journal-only. The structured brief in this issue's comments records the decision, the still-binding constraints and the acceptance criteria.

## Closes when

The owning `STA-20` command-hold text and `STA-24` lost-journal limit explicitly describe this boundary, including overlap during Replace, without bypassing any retained unresolved intent or standing restriction. Preserve advisory evidence, existing collection and all other admission rules. The amendment must not weaken any existing theorem, gate, requirement or assumption boundary. No recovery guard, advisory wait or new dispatch exception is part of this outcome.

Found by the 2026-10-18 grill (tw-k12). The issue remains open for the bounded specification clarification; no normative amendment or integrated result is claimed by triage.

comments.author: triage
comments.text:
## Triage decision and specification amendment brief

**Category:** bug
**Summary:** Make the journal-only limit of command holds explicit after recovery, including the possibility that new work overlaps a command the restored journal does not record.

**Owner decision — 2026-11-01:**
Journal-only. Add no recovery-time record-enumeration check, advisory wait or hold for commands absent from the restored journal. New work after recovery, including model commands, harness-composed check/delivery jobs and Replace's model-free key migration, may overlap an earlier command the restored journal does not record. This is a limit of the chosen protection, not a claim that overlap is safe or that all other admission checks pass.

**Panel split recorded with the decision:**
- Astra: a bounded recovery collection-and-hold guard, to catch observable unfinished work before another command overlaps it.
- Sol: a bounded recovery guard; the restored machine's unchecked state supplies no command-concurrency protection.
- Opus: an operator-cancellable advisory wait; a machine-reported or forged running record must not indefinitely prevent replacing a stolen key.
- Fable: missing seat because of its usage limit.
- Grok: missing seat because of HTTP 402 balance exhaustion.

The owner chose journal-only against those recommendations. This is the owner's decision, not a panel consensus. No guard or advisory-wait design branch remains authorized by this issue.

**Current behavior and the gap to clarify:**
`STA-24` states "The barrier is a fact of the journal — an intent with no terminal record" and "What this rule cannot reach is a journal that is lost with the phone: `STA-14` states that transcripts are gone, and a recovery sheet is not an outstanding-call record." Its current command-hold interpretation likewise derives from surviving intents. The command-hold text needs the corresponding recovery limit made explicit, without weakening that hold for any intent that does survive.

Distinguish total journal loss from an imported local-store backup. A stale backup may retain unresolved intents, terminal records and standing dispositions; the surviving restrictions remain in force. It can also omit later sends. A terminal record collected for one retained intent establishes nothing about another command omitted from the backup. Recovery does not settle a retained unresolved intent, clear its barrier or erase a standing restriction.

**Requirement owners and binding limits:**
- `STA-20` owns the command hold and permitted collection: "Collecting a job record is not held, and other machines are unaffected." State the journal-only limit beside the hold, and point to the existing lost-journal boundary at `STA-24`. Preserve ordinary collection for known calls; rejecting a new recovery-wide check does not remove or prohibit existing permitted reads.
- `STA-8` requires "It MUST NOT be retried automatically and no timer may clear it." `STA-24` supplies the resource barrier and disposition rules. Keep these unchanged for every retained unresolved intent and standing restriction.
- `STA-17` owns Replace. It requires "A machine under `STA-20`'s hold or a standing destructive reinstall or abandonment disposition (`STA-24`) MUST be shown as not yet migrated, with the reason, and MUST keep its old key; Replace migrates the others." Clarify that the absence of a lost intent supplies no additional hold; it does not grant an exemption from a surviving hold or change key-install/confirmation/removal ordering.
- `STA-21` states "The job record is machine-reported and advisory." It also states "The browser journal is authoritative for what was **sent** (`STA-3`, `ARC-8`); the machine's record says what it **received** and what happened next." Retain that boundary. Machine-side enumeration cannot reveal commands that left no record, establish completeness against a hostile machine, reconstruct lost intents or approvals, or promise that an old phone cannot send further work.
- Existing recovery presentation and re-check requirements retain their owners. Explain the chosen overlap limit where recovery and Replace are presented, by referring to its normative owner rather than copying a new rule into several homes. Being unchecked after recovery does not supply the rejected enumeration guard.

**Acceptance criteria:**
- [ ] The owning command-hold and lost-journal text explicitly states journal-only protection and distinguishes full journal loss from an imported backup retaining some unresolved intents.
- [ ] The text explicitly says that new work after recovery, including Replace's model-free key migration, may overlap an earlier command whose send the restored journal does not record. It makes no new concurrency-safety or remote-completeness claim.
- [ ] Every surviving unresolved intent still has its existing hold, reconciliation and disposition behavior. An absent later intent does not release a retained intent or a standing destructive restriction, and settlement of one retained call says nothing about omitted sends.
- [ ] There is no new recovery enumeration prerequisite, advisory wait, orphan-record hold, synthetic intent/approval, new terminal evidence or automatic retry. Existing permitted collection and other admission/output-release checks remain intact.
- [ ] The advisory-record boundary and the inability to discover commands with no record remain explicit. Retain the selected sudo route and its missing-record uncertainty from tw-yuo without turning that route into a recovery check.
- [ ] Check the explanation against the existing journal-derived `openIntents`, command hold and retained-intent/recovery conformance cases. Make only the references or focused coverage needed to demonstrate the chosen boundary; do not invent a conformance guard for the rejected policy.
- [ ] Preserve every existing theorem, gate, requirement and assumption boundary. A theorem is not weakened to make the overlap explanation pass; the explanation must state the knowledge limit the existing guard already has. No new engine or dispatch exception is authorized.
- [ ] Land the rule before recording the rationale, record the rejected guard and advisory-wait alternatives without creating a second normative copy, and run the repository's required gates before and after the amendment. Any new conformance case receives its proper applicability row and tier metadata.

**Readiness and boundaries:**
No further owner policy question remains for this bounded clarification. Keep the issue open and ready-for-agent for specification editing. This triage does not implement the normative amendment or establish live/integrated recovery evidence. Recovery-guard design, new job identity/schema machinery, vendor/machine operations and changes to existing admission or settlement semantics are outside this amendment.

title: OPN-14: does re-entry read running-at-delivery services, and does that lifecycle bind after delivery?
description:
## The question

`OPN-14` leaves two points open:

- "whether `STG-9`'s re-entry re-check reads `running-at-delivery` services, and whether a stopped
  one is then outside its declared lifecycle and hence a lifecycle finding (`CNF-108`)";
- "Whether `running-at-delivery` binds after delivery remains open."

`OPN-14` frames the second: "`ARC-17` says "whenever that read runs — at a delivery check or a
later re-check"; the open point is when that declared lifecycle applies after delivery."

## Why it matters now

`OPN-14` "does block completing the first stage", and the stage-1 re-entry row requires item 108
"before stage 1 completes". Re-entry reads for `enabled-survives-reboot` services are decided:
`ARC-43` says "On re-entry (`STG-9`), read the unit and its enablement for
`enabled-survives-reboot` services." The implementation builds those now. The rest waits as twr-ggw.73, behind the pin
bump twr-ggw.35, and cannot be written until these two points are decided.

## Closes when

Both points are decided in the text that owns them, `OPN-14` no longer lists them as open, and
`T42` agrees.
